items.title: Her Parents Gave Up Two Children to Save Their Lives: Then God Changed Everything
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Powerful.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Miquette McMahon’s mission to educate young Haitians and spread the Gospel began decades ago, when she faced severe poverty and learned firsthand what it means to suffer.

McMahon, founder of Teach Haiti, an organization that provides holistic education to kids in Haiti, told CBN News she grew up in extreme poverty in Haiti and had to fight hard to get an education. Most schools in Haiti are private, and her parents simply couldn’t afford the minimal amount needed to keep her in the classroom.

“My parents desperately wanted their children to have an education even though they never had the opportunity to attend school themselves,” he said. “But I remember the humiliation of being sent home from school because my parents simply could not afford the tuition.”

She recalled being forced to leave school in the 5th grade after not being able to come up with $1 — an experience that has been seared into her brain.

“Imagine being a little girl who loves school, who wants desperately to learn, who wanted to be a nurse, because that was my dream, and be publicly humiliated because your parents could not pay $1,” McMahon said. “I never forget how that felt, and I made a commitment to God [that] if God ever gave me an opportunity, I would do everything I could to prevent another child from experiencing that humiliation that I experienced growing up.”

Over time, she realized that education represented opportunity—something her own parents lacked. McMahon knew education could give her a different, more prosperous future. Ultimately, she said God gave her an education and opportunity, and then used her story to create Teach Haiti.

“God loves His children,” McMahon said. “He wants His children to thrive. At the same time, when God blesses you, He also wants you to be a blessing to others, and I could not keep that gift to myself.”

She created Teach Haiti to honor God and thank Him for all he had done in her life. But the journey to creating the organization came with many twists and turns.

McMahon said severe poverty didn’t only impact her ability to get educated; it also forced her parents to take harrowing steps to protect their children. In 1989, she recalled that two of her siblings were sick all of the time. Her parents kept investing resources to get healing, but they couldn’t find appropriate care. And the family had already suffered great loss.

“My parents had the firstborn die at the age of two-and-a-half from malnutrition,” she said. “And they just simply could not watch losing another child.”

McMahon continued, “They decided to surrender them for adoption in the hope of giving them a life they could not provide.”

The choice was hard, but her parents, who loved the children deeply, felt it was the only way to give them the life they deserved. The family assumed they’d never see the children again — but the Lord had other plans.

“In God’s providence, the father who adopted them visited Haiti in 1989, met my family, met me, learned about my story —especially my dream of becoming a nurse,” she said. “I told them I gave up that dream because I was sent home for $1. I was afraid to dream because I’m like, if my dream could be taken away for just a dollar, then I don’t think I can dream.”

Her siblings’ adoptive family members were moved by her story, so they started looking into ways to bring McMahon to the U.S. as an exchange student. Once that came to fruition, McMahon’s entire life transformed. After getting an education and achieving her dreams, she later started thinking about how she could give back.

“How could you not pay it forward when so many people have given you the chance to be where you are?” McMahon said. “That’s why Teach Haiti was born out of this — that desire to honor God, to really thank Him for what He’s done for me.”

Today, McMahon is educating more than 750 young people in Haiti, describing her organization as a “Christ-centered non-profit organization that believes education is one of the most powerful tools we have to break the cycle of poverty.”

More than a school, the organization focuses on everything from academics to spiritual development and career training.

“We provide a meal every single day for our students,” she said. “They have school supplies, opportunities in music and art, and just guidance for them to become capable leaders, and so we are extremely proud of what we are able to provide our students.”

It’s a powerful service to individuals and families in a nation plagued by natural disasters, chaos, and government malfeasance. With poverty raging, she is offering true opportunity — and welcoming others to help.

“It’s a sponsorship model. Our goal is for every student we have at the school to be matched with a sponsor,” she said. “Forty-five dollars a month, that’s what it takes to change the trajectory of a child’s life through Teach Haiti.”

McMahon is hoping people join her to help Haitians find opportunity and success.

“Our goal is to develop a generation of Haitians who can help transform their own country, and I believe that was a responsibility for me as a Haitian to say we cannot wait for America, for other countries to come save our [country],” she said. “We need to use the gift that God has given and to be able to make an impact for our own country as well.

Find out more about Teach Haiti.

items.title: It’s Time to Rethink How You Read the Bible, Chicago Pastor Says
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "The Word of God is the living seed that actually brings new life."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

With the Christmas season kicking into high gear and a new year around the corner, many Christians are starting to think about spiritual disciplines, about setting goals of reading through the Bible and establishing practical ways to prioritize spending time with God. For some, though, diving into the pages of Scripture can feel intimidating and overwhelming.

Chicago-area Pastor Colin Smith, a native of Edinburgh, Scotland, recently appeared on CBN’s “Faith in Culture,” where he explained the importance of understanding what the Bible is meant to do: not simply inform us, but transform us.

“I try in conversations … to guide people away from thinking that the Bible is essentially information,” he said. “The Word of God is the living seed that actually brings new life.”

Smith, who recently stepped down as senior pastor of The Orchard Evangelical Free Church in Arlington Heights, Illinois, after a 30-year tenure, is the author of three guides to read through Scripture, “Fly Through the Bible,” “Drive Through the Bible,” and “Hike Through the Bible.”

After leaving Edinburgh, Smith moved to London to study theology and then spent 16 years in ministry there, before moving to Chicago. His experience across several cultures, he said, reinforced his belief that, despite human beings’ differences, their deepest need is universal.

“The differences are significant, but they are actually superficial,” he explained. “The wonderful thing to me is that the Word of God speaks directly to every person in every culture, in every generation — and that never changes.”

Smith’s three guides through the Bible — “Fly,” “Drive,” and “Hike” — are associated with his ministry, Open the Bible, and each provides a different entry point into studying Scripture, helping readers understand God’s story of redemption, as Smith says, “from the garden to the city.”

“Fly Through the Bible” gives readers a broad overview through five Old Testament figures, five significant events in Jesus’ earthly life, and five gifts God grants to believers. “Drive Through the Bible” expands that framework into a 30-day devotional and “Hike Through the Bible” takes readers through 50 chapters over the course of one year, a study Smith intended for small groups or personal discipleship.

Part of what can make Scripture reading so burdensome is the feeling of needing to perfectly understand every detail of the text. Smith warned against allowing that to become a barrier to digging into the Bible.

“Read something and look for something that you can take into your mind and heart and carry with you, kinda chew on, meditate on during the day, make your own, and seek to kind of live on it,” said Smith.

Gloo and Barna Group has released data showing weekly Bible reading is trending upward. In 2025, Scripture reading among U.S. adults climbed to 42% — a 12-point increase from a 15-year low of 30% in 2024. And among self-identified Christians, the rate is 50%, the highest level in more than a decade. Interestingly, though, Lifeway Research recently polled more than 2,000 American Christian churchgoers with dozens of questions on general Bible knowledge, about 65% scored below 60%. So, while there has been an uptick in Scripture interest, that has not necessarily correlated to greater awareness.

But Smith wasn’t discouraged, reiterating that believers’ goals shouldn’t be to win trivia contests. Instead, they should see Scripture as a tool for understanding and knowing the character of God, and allowing that to shape their thinking, feelings, and daily lives.

“It’s not simply learning a book; this is the word of God,” he said. “This is how God speaks to you.”

Smith encouraged believers to be willing to step into discomfort in reading Scripture. He pointed to Paul, who wrote in 2 Corinthians 12:10, “For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong” (ESV). The pastor pointed out that Paul was certainly not weak to begin with, having endured imprisonment, beatings, and three shipwrecks. What the apostle was getting at, Smith explained, was that God often calls us to act in obedience when the tasks He hands us are overwhelming.

“Jesus doesn’t want us to splash around in the shallows,” Smith said. “He wants us to launch out into the deep.”

That has been a central part of Smith’s own life. He recalled a letter he received from a professor and mentor when he was considering becoming a pastor. The professor wrote to Smith: “If you do this you will soon find yourself out of your depth, and you will prove God in ways you never thought possible.”

“I think that’s the story of my life,” Smith reflected.

Listen to our full conversation with Pastor Colin Smith in the “Faith in Culture” podcast above.

items.title: Houses of Horror: The Mistreatment of the Vulnerable
items.author: Mark Bradford
items.summary:
Mark Bradford

The ongoing abuse and neglect of vulnerable persons that hides behind a facade of compassion is a human tragedy and should be an area of grave concern for the Church.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Mark Bradford

On January 7, 1972, the journalist Geraldo Rivera was escorted into Willowbrook State School in Staten Island, NY, by a recently fired employee. This man had invited him, hoping that he would reveal the horrors existing within the state-run facility for the developmentally disabled. Rivera and his crew were horrified by what they found. He reported that you could describe what you see and hear, but there is no way to describe the smell. He said, “It smelled of filth, it smelled of disease, and it smelled of death.”

Rivera’s documentary Willowbrook: The Last Great Disgrace aired on February 2, 1972, and became the catalyst that finally, in 1987, closed one of America’s largest and most notorious institutions that housed and allegedly educated people with developmental disabilities. At the time of Rivera’s filming, there were almost 5,300 individuals living in Willowbrook in squalid conditions—often naked and sitting in their own waste. Some physicians used the residents as lab specimens, intentionally infecting them with hepatitis to study the disease and methods of preventing it. Their justification was that many children who lived there would develop hepatitis anyway. 

Many thought that the end of Willowbrook would be the end of the practice of warehousing vulnerable individuals in large institutions and the abuse that was rampant within them. But was it? Sadly, no. More than fifty years after the Willowbook exposé, the abuse and neglect of vulnerable persons remains a national disgrace and provides an opportunity for the Church, whose commitment to the dignity and protection of vulnerable persons beckons an appropriate response.

Some good did come from Rivera’s reporting. The public exposure of Willowbrook inspired state legislation to protect residents of other facilities in New York, and protective legislation was also passed at the federal level. In 1975, Congress passed the Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act that established protection and advocacy systems that provided for investigations into abuse by independent agencies. And in 1980, the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act authorized the Justice Department to investigate and sue over systemic violations of federal rights in state and local institutions. A key decision in 1999 from the US Supreme Court, Olmstead v. L.C., ruled that the unjustified institutionalization of persons with disabilities is a form of discrimination, depriving individuals of ordinary opportunities for family relationships, friendships, work, and cultural participation.

A family advocacy organization called Voice of Reason believes, “Community placement cannot and should not be treated as mandatory for every individual,” and individuals and their families should “have a right to choose the setting that best meets individual needs, whether that is a family home, supported living, community-based program, intermediate care facility (ICF), or another specialized residential option.” Willowbrook’s disgrace hastened a shift away from large institutional facilities to more home and community-based services. In 2024, thirty-two states were still operating large congregate residential facilities that housed sixteen or more individuals—but the size of the facility doesn’t matter as much as the care it provides. No setting should be presumed safe or unsafe based solely on its size and classification. Risk is not determined only by size; it is determined by management, oversight of facilities, funding, and staffing. Abuse and neglect can exist even in smaller group housing.

Willowbrook’s notoriety made it synonymous with the institutional cruelty individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities suffered—but Willowbrook wasn’t the only such institution. Pennhurst in Pennsylvania, Fairview Training Center in Oregon, and Rosewood Center in Maryland were others where prejudice, discrimination, physical and sexual abuse, and neglect were rampant. But the transition to group homes and community-based care facilities hasn’t solved the problem. As recently as 2018, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) reported systemic concerns of health and safety in group homes in forty-nine of our fifty states.

To provide current examples from just one state, in 2022 ProPublica, Capitol News Illinois, and Lee Enterprises all documented staff assaults and a pattern of mistreatment at Choate Developmental Center, a state-run facility in Illinois. One reported incident involved a twenty-four-year-old with developmental disabilities who was brutally beaten by his caretakers inside this house of horrors. After more than two thousand hours of monitoring and review, the following year, Equip for Equality revealed continuing harm to residents at Choate, citing staff who witnessed abuse and allowed it to continue without intervening—even helping to conceal it.

Choate is just one of the three Illinois facilities the DOJ announced in 2025 was under investigation for abuse and neglect. The state of Illinois runs seven of these facilities, and I know personally of a fourth that should be added to the DOJ’s list.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Joseph is a thirty-three-year-old man with autism, intellectual disability, and a seizure disorder. He lives at an Illinois state-run facility that is not currently under investigation. His guardian has documented and reported many instances of him being abused by staff, some of which have resulted in visits to a hospital emergency room for treatment. But repeated requests for a place of safety for Joseph have been ignored by the facility’s administration.

In March 2026, an exam conducted in the emergency department verified that Joseph had been raped, and the most likely perpetrator, because of restricted access, was a member of the staff. The hospital reported the rape to the Illinois State Police who opened a criminal investigation. However, as I write this eight months later, the perpetrator has not been identified. The administration still refuses to secure Joseph’s safety, even after his guardians obtained a court order with a “Demand for Immediate Compliance,” to three specific protections. Instead of complying, the administration moved the other residents out of Joseph’s building and placed another man in his house—a man with a reputation for aggressive behavior. His new housemate has been seen on camera covering the security cameras with a towel, stealing his property, and beating Joseph with a curtain rod. Still, nothing changes, and Joseph is left with the trauma of abuse. 

Joseph is one person, living in one facility, in one state. I only know of him because I know his guardian. How many more Josephs might there be who are unknown and hidden out of sight, suffering daily abuse and neglect in facilities that have been licensed to care for them? The HHS Office of Inspector General has called the problem of abuse in these places “systemic.”

The Willowbrook exposé, documentary, news reports that revealed the horrors, attempts at reform, and the laws passed to protect residents all seem to have solved little. An audit of the Connecticut Department of Developmental Services revealed that 151 of 152 “critical incidents” of potential abuse or neglect in group homes had not been reported to the state’s Office of Protection and Advocacy.

Systemic abuse on this scale reveals massive organizational failure. The structures, policies, oversight, and culture in some of these places preserve an environment of harm where criminal neglect and abuse of vulnerable individuals continues with impunity. Inadequate staffing ratios, poor pay, and the lack of scrupulous hiring policies, training, oversight design, and accountability may explain why incidents are not investigated, reported, and remedied. Where is the solution?

In Pope Leo’s first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, he affirms the “distinction between the ecclesial community and the political community, emphasizing that each must operate with full autonomy” (21). However, he also notes that “when the dignity of our brothers and sisters is violated, when politics fails to address the tragedies of humanity . . . the Church—together with other Christian denominations and believers of other religions—must make her voice heard” (27). During the Holy Father’s recent trip to South America, he met and spoke in support of vulnerable individuals, especially in Argentina where financial support for their care has been reduced as part of the government’s austerity measures.

Without a doubt, there are many care facilities in the US that are doing an excellent job of providing for the needs of their residents. However, the systemic problems in others have not been solved by current laws and regulations. The ongoing abuse and neglect of vulnerable persons that hides behind a facade of compassion is a human tragedy and should be an area of grave concern for the Church.

The Catholic Church has always responded generously to the needs of the vulnerable, but its capacity is limited. To cite one example, in the Archdiocese of Chicago, Misericordia Home can accommodate more than 650 individuals in their campus and community-based settings, but in 2024, Misericordia reported that they had more than 600 families still in its applicant pool waiting for admission. 

The Church’s moral responsibility to care for the vulnerable doesn’t only apply to those who can be accommodated in Catholic institutions. Wherever institutional neglect and abuse of vulnerable persons occurs, the Church is called to make its voice heard. As Pope Leo said in Argentina, “A nation’s progress is . . . measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs,” or as Pope St. John Paul II framed the same message in 1998, the “degree of civilization is measured by the protection given to the weakest members of the social fabric.” Both popes were drawing from the words of Christ in Matt 25:45–46 that we have come to call the Corporal Works of Mercy. We know Jesus’s harsh words for those who failed to care for the hungry, thirsty, naked, sick, strangers, and imprisoned. The cost of failure to care for those in need is grave.

What can the Church do? I would suggest three possible areas where the Church could intervene:

Expose

Catholic journalists and diocesan communications offices should investigate credible allegations and report on failures to protect vulnerable persons.

Advocate

State Catholic conferences should make the protection of persons with intellectual and developmental disabilities a legislative priority, advocating for independent investigations into abuse, enforceable safeguards, and protection against retaliation for whistleblowers.

Accompany

Parishes and dioceses should support families and guardians who struggle to secure the safety of their loved ones and help them to navigate public agencies and obtain appropriate legal and advocacy assistance. No one should be left alone to face a system that allows for the abuse, mistreatment, or neglect of their loved ones who have no option other than to reside in facilities.

Of course, as Catholics, we believe foremost in the importance of intercessory prayer. Please pray for Joseph and all others who are hidden away in institutions and suffer abuse or neglect. Pray for their families whose desperate efforts to protect their loved ones are thwarted by systems whose priority is to protect rather than provide loving and humane care for the weak and vulnerable.

Madison Ayers

Bringing people together, crafting a meal that makes them feel welcomed and cared for, and enjoying people you love over the dinner table are core parts of what it means to be a person.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Madison Ayers

The first year it was just eight of us in a junior’s college apartment. I don’t remember whose idea it was to have a Thanksgiving dinner for our little club of friends (AKA, Friendsgiving), but I quickly took over the project as the most capable cook in the group. On the last weekend before Thanksgiving break, I spent my Saturday prepping pies, cooking sides, and laying the table for a bunch of college students whose typical idea of hosting was buying an extra six-pack for a dorm room party. 

Boxed stuffing and frozen dinner rolls notwithstanding, everyone agreed that it was one of their favorite meals in a long time. When dinner was over, I remember sitting there and thinking that I had never felt more accomplished and important than I had in that evening when I fed people I loved and treated them like they mattered. I was nineteen and had academic achievements at that point, but none of them felt as real as this moment did. 

We did Friendsgiving for two more years, each year bigger than the last. My sophomore year, I fed just under twenty friends, and that year, I had the help of my roommate and my then-boyfriend, now husband. I built a shopping list and cooking plan weeks in advance, made a variety of pies, and again felt a complete high by the end of it. The final year, I enlisted more girlfriends to help and tried to impart my Friendsgiving-hosting wisdom on them in hopes that the event would continue after I graduated. We fed over thirty people together that day.

A decade after that first Friendsgiving, I have cooked more Thanksgiving meals (the real thing now!) and many other meals besides. I’ve made intricate dinners for my husband and I in our first year of marriage when time abounded, quick and easy meals for our family of four, intimate dinner parties,  large-scale events with friends, and everything in between. 

There is a lot to be said about the importance of family dinners and sitting down with your immediate family each night around the table, but I fear the act of cooking for other people is quickly fading from our cultural reality. A little more than half of Americans either attended or threw a dinner party in the past year, with just two-thirds having people over in their homes socially at all. These numbers are in a free-fall from the 1990s, and you can guess where all of the extra time is going. We are seeing the death of hosting with no sign of improvement. 

The loss of authentic community, replaced by digital “leisure,” is a virus that has propagated the loneliness epidemic we are currently experiencing. One of the symptoms of this disease is losing out on one of the most simple yet sublime gifts to humanity: getting to love someone through food. Bringing people together, crafting a meal that makes them feel welcomed and cared for, and enjoying people you love over the dinner table are core parts of what it means to be a person. 

Our Lord himself hosted a dinner party with his closest friends on the night before his passion. Don’t you think, on that night, he lovingly chose everything that was to be served and delighted in the company of his friends as they shared in food and wine? Christ chose the setting of a dinner as the place of the institution of the Eucharist to show us that we are not merely animals who have instincts to feed ourselves nor machines who need “food as fuel” like a car needs gas, but that we are fully human, and eating with one another is sacramental in its very nature. 

Creating home-cooked food out of real ingredients, laboring over a meal, and giving of our time and talents are not mere chores but a way for us to participate in communion with one another. We commune at the dinner table as a reminder of the heavenly Communion we receive at the Sunday liturgy, where the Church feeds us in her love and compassion. 

As modern people, we are struggling with this. This is easily displayed by statistics that show Americans spend well over $3000 annually on eating out, around 40 percent of the total amount we spend on food. Grocery stores have devoted more of their floor space to single-serving, ready-made meals, and most people are eating at least one meal in their car each week, with Gen Z averaging almost four meals consumed in their car weekly—most likely alone. We’re swimming in the decadence of rapid availability of every variety and flavor of food unimaginable but drowning in the loss of the community that used to be served alongside.

Where do we go from here? We again turn to the example Christ sets: a table, laid with food, surrounded by friends. We begin with creating a meal, however imperfect, and inviting others to sit around the table and share in it with us. This may start with instituting regular family mealtimes, but it should not end there. You must reach out into your community and invite others into your home and cook for them. This may be close friends or family members, but ideally, it should extend out to the couple at your church who recently got married, the coworkers you want to get to know better, or even your actual neighbors. You don’t need to be wealthy or own a large home to host; many of our first dinner parties were hosted in a small apartment with simple ingredients. 

Once you’ve invited them, lay a feast. This may be an actual feast (lesser-celebrated liturgical holidays like the Nativity of Mary or the Annunciation are a great option for this) or a simple Saturday night dinner with a roasted chicken and salad. Don’t feel the need to attempt something above what you’re capable of, but resist the temptation to just order a pizza. Make something real—labor over the stove and create something with your own two hands that you can stand over with pride as you all sit down to pray. Make enough so everyone can have second helpings, receive compliments with grace, and squeeze in more people than you thought possible around your table. 

Last month, my husband and I hosted some of our old college friends (some of whom attended that first Friendsgiving) and their families for breakfast. It was raining, so we couldn’t be outside as we originally planned. Instead, we all squeezed into our relatively small kitchen and living room. Many of us sat on the floor, the older children went outside to play in the rain, and we had four babies total in attendance. We made breakfast tacos with coffee and muffins, which were quickly devoured by all.

In many ways, it was chaos, and nineteen-year-old me wouldn’t have believed that I somehow pulled it off—this time with a toddler and preschooler as my “helpers” rather than a small pack of college girls. But I experienced the exact same feeling of love and accomplishment at the end of the gathering as I did nearly a decade ago. In a small way, I was able to be Christ to those I loved by serving them a warm plate of something homemade, looking at them across the table (or living room floor), and loving them. This means of grace is available to all of us just by opening up our homes and setting the table for communion.
